zh:
【公食大夫礼第九】

公食大夫之礼。使大夫戒，各以其爵。上介出请，入告。三辞。宾出，拜辱。大夫不答拜，将命。宾再拜稽首。大夫还，宾不拜送，遂从之。宾朝服即位于大门外，如聘。
即位，具。羹定，甸人陈鼎七，当门，南面西上，设扃鼏，鼏若束若编。设洗如飨。小臣具槃匜，在东堂下。宰夫设筵，加席、几。无尊。饮酒、浆饮，俟于东房。凡宰夫之具，馔于东房。
公如宾服迎宾于大门内。大夫纳宾。宾入门左，公再拜；宾辟，再拜稽首。公揖入，宾从。及庙门，公揖入。宾入，三揖。至于阶，三让。公升二等，宾升。大夫立于东夹南，西面北上。士立于门东，北面西上。小臣，东堂下，南面西上。宰，东夹北，西面南上。内官之士在宰东北，西面南上。介，门西，北面西上。公当楣北乡，至壹拜，宾降也，公再拜。宾，西阶东，北面答拜。摈者辞，拜也；公降一等。辞曰：「寡君从子，虽将拜，兴也！」宾粟阶升，不拜，命之成拜，阶上北面再拜稽首。
士举鼎，去鼏于外，次于。陈鼎于碑南，南面西上。右人抽扃，坐奠于鼎西南，顺出自鼎西，左人待载。雍人以俎入，陈于鼎南。旅人南面加匕于鼎，退。大人长盥洗东南，西面北上，序进盥。退者与进者交于前。卒盥，序进，南面匕。载者西面。鱼腊饪。载体进奏。鱼七，缩俎，寝右。肠、胃七，同俎。伦肤七。肠、胃、肤，皆横诸俎，垂之。大夫既匕，匕奠于鼎，逆退，复位。
公降盥，宾降，公辞。卒盥，公壹揖壹让。公升，宾升。宰夫自东房授醯酱，公设之。宾辞，北面坐迁而东迁所。公立于序内，西乡。宾立于阶西，疑立。宰夫自东房荐豆六，设于酱东，西上，韭菹，以东醓醢、昌本；昌本南麋臡以西菁菹、鹿臡。士设俎于豆南，西上，牛、羊、豕，鱼在牛南，腊、肠、胃亚之，肤以为特。旅人取匕，甸人举鼎，顺出，奠于其所。宰夫设黍、稷六簋于俎西，二以并，东北上。黍当牛俎，其西稷，错以终，南陈。大羹湆，不和，实于镫。宰右执镫，左执盖，由门入，升自阼阶，尽阶，不升堂，授公，以盖降，出，入反位。公设之于酱西，宾辞，坐迁之。宰夫设鉶四于豆西，东上，牛以西羊，羊南豕豕以东牛。饮酒，实于觯，加于丰。宰夫右执觯，左执丰，进设于豆东。宰夫东面，坐启簋会，各却于其西。赞者负东房，南面，告具于公。
……
en:
【The Rites of the Host Feasting the Envoy, Chapter IX】

The rite of the host feasting the envoy: He sends a high officer to announce the feast, each according to his rank. The attendant goes out to receive the message, then enters to report. After three refusals, the guest comes out and bows in acknowledgment of the honor. The high officer does not return the bow but delivers the message. The guest bows twice with his head to the ground. The high officer departs, and the guest does not bow to see him off but follows him. The guest, in court robes, takes his position outside the main gate, as in the聘 rite.
After taking positions, preparations are made. When the broth is ready, the officer in charge of the grounds arranges seven cauldrons, facing the gate, with their handles to the south and arranged from west to east, setting the crossbars and covers, the covers either tied or woven. The washing basin is set up as in the banquet rite. The minor officials prepare the basin and ewer, placing them at the east of the hall. The steward sets out the mats, adding additional mats and an armrest. No wine vessel is placed. The wine and rice drink are kept waiting in the eastern chamber. All the steward's utensils are arranged in the eastern chamber.
The duke, in the guest's robes, welcomes the guest inside the main gate. The high officer introduces the guest. The guest enters to the left of the gate; the duke bows twice; the guest steps aside and bows twice with his head to the ground. The duke bows and enters, and the guest follows. At the temple gate, the duke bows and enters. The guest enters, and they exchange three bows. At the steps, they yield three times. The duke ascends two steps, and the guest ascends. The high officers stand to the south of the eastern wing, facing west, with the most noble to the north. The officers stand to the east of the gate, facing north, with the most noble to the west. The minor officials are at the east of the hall, facing south, with the most noble to the west. The steward is to the north of the eastern wing, facing west, with the most noble to the south. The inner officers are to the northeast of the steward, facing west, with the most noble to the south. The attendants stand to the west of the gate, facing north, with the most noble to the west. The duke, facing the ridge beam and looking north, bows once; the guest descends, and the duke bows twice. The guest, to the east of the western steps, faces north and returns the bow. The usher declines the bow and says, "My lord follows you; even though he wishes to bow, rise!" The guest ascends the steps without bowing, and the duke commands him to complete the bow; the guest, on the steps facing north, bows twice with his head to the ground.
The officers lift the cauldrons, removing the covers outside, and place them in order. The cauldrons are arranged to the south of the stele, facing south, with the most noble to the west. The men on the right remove the crossbars, sit and place them to the southwest of the cauldrons, then withdraw from the west of the cauldrons; the men on the left wait to load the food. The cook brings in the meat stands and places them to the south of the cauldrons. The attendants, facing south, place the ladles in the cauldrons and withdraw. The senior officers wash their hands to the southeast of the washing basin, facing west, with the most noble to the north, and proceed in order to wash. Those withdrawing and those advancing cross in front. After washing, they proceed in order, facing south, and ladle out the food. Those loading face west. The fish and dried meat are cooked. The meat is presented with the front facing forward. Seven fish are placed lengthwise on the stands, lying on their right sides. Seven sets of intestines and stomachs are placed on the same stand. Seven pieces of skin and fat are placed. The intestines, stomachs, and skin are all laid across the stands, hanging over the edges. After the high officers have ladled, they place the ladles back in the cauldrons and withdraw in reverse order, returning to their positions.
The duke descends to wash his hands, and the guest descends; the duke declines. After washing, the duke makes one bow and one yielding gesture. The duke ascends, and the guest ascends. The steward, from the eastern chamber, hands over the vinegar and paste, and the duke places them. The guest declines, then sits facing north, moves them, and shifts them to the east. The duke stands within the screen, facing west. The guest stands to the west of the steps, standing still. The steward, from the eastern chamber, presents six dishes of pickled vegetables, placing them to the east of the vinegar, with the most noble to the west: leek pickles, then to the east meat sauce and昌本; south of昌本 is deer paste, and to the west are celery pickles and deer paste. The officers place the meat stands to the south of the dishes, with the most noble to the west: beef, mutton, and pork; fish is to the south of the beef, and dried meat, intestines, and stomachs follow, with skin and fat as a separate offering. The attendants take the ladles, and the officer in charge of the grounds lifts the cauldrons, withdrawing in order and placing them in their proper positions. The steward sets out six vessels of millet and rice to the west of the meat stands, in pairs, with the most noble to the northeast. The millet is placed opposite the beef stand, with rice to its west, alternating to the end, arranged to the south. The great broth, unseasoned, is placed in a vessel. The steward holds the vessel in his right hand and the lid in his left, enters through the gate, ascends by the eastern steps, and when he reaches the top, without entering the hall, hands it to the duke, then descends with the lid, exits, and returns to his position. The duke places it to the west of the vinegar; the guest declines and, sitting, moves it. The steward sets out four tripod vessels to the west of the dishes, with the most noble to the east: beef to the west of mutton, mutton to the south of pork, and pork to the east of beef. The wine is poured into a goblet and placed on a stand. The steward, holding the goblet in his right hand and the stand in his left, advances and places them to the east of the dishes. The steward, facing east, sits and opens the covers of the vessels, each placed to its west. The assistant, with his back to the eastern chamber, faces south and reports to the duke that everything is ready.
……

【述而第七】

子曰：“述而不作，信而好古，窃比于我老彭。”
子曰：“默而识之，学而不厌，诲人不倦，何有于我哉？”
子曰：“德之不修也，学之不讲也，闻义不能从也，不善不能改也，是吾忧也。”
子之燕居，申申如也，夭夭如也。
子曰：“甚矣，吾衰也。久矣，吾不复梦见周公也。”
子曰：“志于道，据于德，依于仁，游于艺。”
子曰：“自行束修以上，吾未尝无诲焉。”
子曰：“不愤不启，不悱不发，举一隅而示之，不以三隅反，则吾不复。”
子食于有丧者之侧，未尝饱也。子于是日也哭，则不歌。
子谓颜渊曰：“用之则行，舍之则藏，唯我与尔有是夫。”子路曰：“子行三军，则谁与？”子曰：“暴虎凭河，死而无悔者，吾不与也，必也临事而惧，好谋而成者也。”
子曰：“富而可求也，虽执鞭之士，吾亦为之。如不可求者，从吾所好。”
子之所慎：齐、战、疾。
子在齐闻韶乐，三月不知肉味，曰：“不图为乐之至于斯也。”
冉有曰：“夫子为卫君乎？”子贡曰：“诺。吾将问之。”入，曰：“伯夷、叔齐，何人也？”子曰：“古之贤人也。”曰：“怨乎？曰：“求仁而得仁，又何怨乎？”出，曰：“夫子不为也。”
子曰：“饭蔬食，饮水，曲肱而枕之，乐亦在其中矣。不义而富且贵，于我如浮云。”
子曰：“加我数年，五十以学易，可以无大过矣。”
子所雅言，诗、书、执礼，皆雅言也。
叶公问孔子于子路，子路不对。子曰：“女奚不曰：“其为人也，发愤忘食，乐以忘忧，不知老之将至也云尔。”
子曰：“我非生而知之者，好古，敏而求之者也。”
子不语，怪、力、乱、神。
子曰：“三人行，必得我师焉，择其善者而从之，其不善者而改之。”
子曰：“天生德于予，桓魋其如予何？”
子曰：“二三子以我为隐子乎？吾无隐乎尔。吾无所行而不与二三子者，是丘也。”
子以四教：文、行、忠、信。
子曰：“圣人，吾不得而见之矣。得见君子者，斯可矣。”
子曰：“善人，吾不得而见之矣。 得见有恒者，斯可矣。亡而为有，虚而为盈，约而为泰，难乎有恒矣。”
子钓而不纲，弋不射宿。
子曰：“盖有不知而作之者，我无是也。多闻，择其善者而从之。多见而识之，知次也。”
互乡难与言。童子见，门人惑。子曰：“与其进也，不与其退也。唯何甚人洁已以进，与其洁也，不保其往也。”

en:
[Chapter 7: Transmission]

The Master said, "A transmitter and not a maker, believing in and loving the ancients, I venture to compare myself with our old Peng."
The Master said, "The silent treasuring up of knowledge; learning without satiety; and instructing others without being wearied—what one of these things belongs to me?"
The Master said, "The leaving virtue without proper cultivation; the not thoroughly discussing what is learned; not being able to move towards righteousness of which a knowledge is gained; and not being able to change what is not good—these are the things which occasion me solicitude."
When the Master was unoccupied with business, his manner was easy, and he looked pleased.
The Master said, "Extreme is my decay. For a long time, I have not dreamed, as I was wont to do, that I saw the Duke of Zhou."
The Master said, "Let the will be set on the path of duty. Let every attainment in what is good be firmly grasped. Let perfect virtue be accorded with. Let relaxation and enjoyment be found in the polite arts."
The Master said, "From the person bringing one's bundle of dried flesh for my teaching upwards, I have never refused instruction to anyone."
The Master said, "I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge, nor help out anyone who is not anxious to explain oneself. When I have presented one corner of a subject to anyone, and one cannot from it learn the other three, I do not repeat my lesson."
When the Master was eating by the side of a mourner, he never ate to the full. He did not sing on the same day in which he had been weeping.
The Master said to Yan Yuan, "When called to office to undertake its duties; when not so called, to lie retired—it is only I and you who have attained to this." Zilu said, "If you had the conduct of the armies of a great state, whom would you have to act with you?" The Master said, "I would not have one to act with me, who will unarmed attack a tiger, or cross a river without a boat, dying without any regret. My associate must be the person who proceeds to action full of solicitude, who is fond of adjusting one's plans, and then carries them into execution."
The Master said, "If the search for riches is sure to be successful, though I should become a groom with whip in hand to get them, I will do so. As the search may not be successful, I will follow after that which I love."
The things in reference to which the Master exercised the greatest caution were—fasting, war, and sickness.
When the Master was in Qi, he heard the Shao, and for three months did not know the taste of flesh. "I did not think," he said, "that music could have been made so excellent as this."
Ran You said, "Is our Master for the prince of Wei?" Zigong said, "Oh! I will ask him." He went in accordingly, and said, "What sort of people were Boyi and Shuqi?" "They were ancient worthies," said the Master. "Did they have any repinings because of their course?" The Master again replied, "They sought to act virtuously, and they did so; what was there for them to repine about?" On this, Zigong went out and said, "Our Master is not for him."
The Master said, "With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow—I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness are to me as a floating cloud."
The Master said, "If some years were added to my life, I would give fifty to the study of the Yi, and then I might come to be without great faults."
The Master's frequent themes of discourse were—the Odes, the History, and the maintenance of the Rules of propriety. On all these he frequently discoursed.
The duke of She asked Zilu about Confucius, and Zilu did not answer him. The Master said, "Why did you not say to him—He is simply a person, who in his eager pursuit of knowledge forgets his food, who in the joy of its attainment forgets his sorrows, and who does not perceive that old age is coming on?"
The Master said, "I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there."
The subjects on which the Master did not talk, were—extraordinary things, feats of strength, disorder, and spiritual beings.
The Master said, "When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them."
The Master said, "Heaven produced the virtue that is in me. Huan Tui—what can he do to me?"
The Master said, "Do you think, my disciples, that I have any concealments? I conceal nothing from you. There is nothing which I do that is not shown to you, my disciples—that is my way."
There were four things which the Master taught—letters, ethics, devotion of soul, and truthfulness.
The Master said, "A sage it is not mine to see; could I see a person of real talent and virtue, that would satisfy me."
The Master said, "A good person it is not mine to see; could I see a person possessed of constancy, that would satisfy me. Having not and yet affecting to have, empty and yet affecting to be full, straitened and yet affecting to be at ease—it is difficult with such characteristics to have constancy."
The Master angled—but did not use a net. He shot—but not at birds perching.
The Master said, "There may be those who act without knowing why. I do not do so. Hearing much and selecting what is good and following it, seeing much and keeping it in memory—this is the second style of knowledge."
It was difficult to talk with the people of Huxiang, and a lad of that place having had an interview with the Master, the disciples doubted. The Master said, "I admit people's approach to me without committing myself as to what they may do when they have retired. Why must one be so severe? If a person purify oneself to wait upon me, I receive one so purified, without guaranteeing one's past conduct."

它最爱和小主人一起玩“跳高高”的游戏，不管主人把手举多高，跳跳总能一跃而起，稳稳够着。
日子一天天过去，小主人慢慢长大，跳跳也从小狗变成了老狗。
主人不再像之前整日陪着它。他白天总会出门，直到晚上才回来，回来时还一边叹气一边捶着腰，看起来累极了。
而每次离开家前，他都会回头望跳跳一眼。一开始，跳跳以为要玩跳高高，它努力想跳起来，却没什么力气。可主人没有把手举高，只是每天离开时，都会弯下腰，轻轻抱抱它。
en:
Jumper was a stray who found his purpose as a guard dog. He still carries the faint memory of that rainy night when a boy carried him home. The house was warm, dry, and smelled of meat. Jumper had only ever watched such a place from a distance, never daring to approach.
His favorite game with the boy was "Jump High." No matter how high the little hand reached, Jumper would leap and tap it, steady every time.
Years passed. The boy grew up, and Jumper went from pup to old dog. His master no longer stayed home all day. He left each morning and returned at night, sighing, rubbing his back, worn thin by the world.
But every day before leaving, he would look back at Jumper. At first, Jumper thought it was time for Jump High; he'd try to leap, though his strength was failing. But his master never raised his hand. Instead, each morning, he bent down and held Jumper close.

en: In Jiangnan, there exists a poisonous Shegong insect, also called Short Fox or Yu, commonly found in mountain streams. It has a transverse bone in its mouth, shaped like a curved bow. Its body is jet-black, resembling a large cockroach. It has teeth and hair and exists in male and female forms. The males bear two horns at the mouth with jointed tips that can flex. In winter, they burrow underground and emit a rising vapor; snow falling on them melts without sticking. In summer, they dwell in water. When people walk through streams or bathe in natural waters, or during floods, they may enter homes or linger in hoofprints along paths. It is said that when they "spit sand at a person's shadow," sickness soon follows.

I looked everywhere, and what did I find? A cold stove, a wide-open window, and a few loose feathers! The only thing left was a note pinned to the cutting board with a couple of claw marks that said, 
"It's a day of respite! Work can wait! I'll be going to Qingzhou to hang out with the hometown couriers."
Whatever. It's a day of respite for everyone. All the offices are shut down, and even the Emperor said everyone should take a breather. I can't really get too mad at Windtail for slacking off. It does work its tail feathers off in that kitchen usually...
So, what are your plans for the holiday? Since you've got time off, why not take a trip down to Qingzhou yourself? If you manage to catch that runaway bird, grab it by the tail feathers and make it treat you to some good food and fun! As it said, work can always wait.)

zh:
顾盼姐，久别无恙？

我这儿攒的新鲜事呀，可快把我憋坏了。白日里还有小莲能听我说几句，可她就只会点头，摇头，点头，摇头，况且我想说的话，连她也听不得。我只得夜里偷摸记几笔，写完自己读两遍，又不得已地丢进炭火盆了。不过那纸灰飘起来，影影绰绰，倒也算有个回应。
好在这回与往日都不同，信里再无甚与燕北盟相关的要事，姐姐定然就舍不得烧了，只得小心地找个匣子供起来——正好遂了我的愿！
姐姐说不定觉得蹊跷，战事当前，滹沱河边的契丹人同那小蜚蠊似的，踩死一脚能冒出一窝，怎会反而无信可书？
噫，全因丁香近日得了个惊天大秘闻，揣在心里也震得人惶惶，可厉害了！
但我偏不告诉姐姐。谁叫姐姐往日总嫌我闲话多得像车毂，总也转不到个头。如今我可学乖啦，什么也不说。反正天高地远，姐姐亦不知我此刻在哪座房檐下絮叨，急得跺脚也捉不着人，只能干着急啦。
丁香向来是崇拜姐姐的，既能顾着祁家庄子，又能顾着从商修道，得了颇多信任，就连那边境一带，都常听百姓提起姐姐呢！丁香听了可骄傲了，心里比饮了蜜还甜。
不过很快，我也要名动天下啦。待此番事了，将来那戏台子上演的群英传，茶馆里说的风云录，街头巷尾卖的话本子，全都会写满我丁香的大名。
姐姐且等着瞧好了吧！
en:
Sister Gu Pan, I trust you have been well since we last parted?

I have so much fresh gossip bottled up here that I am nearly fit to burst. In the daytime, there is at least Xiao Lian to listen to me for a few words, but all she ever does is nod, shake her head, nod, shake her head. Besides, the things I most want to say are exactly the things even she must not be allowed to hear. So I have had no choice but to sneak away at night and scribble down a few lines in secret. Once I finish, I read them over twice to myself, then throw them into the brazier anyway. Still, when the ashes curl up into the air, it almost feels as though something is answering back.
But this time is different. There is nothing in this letter about the Northern Vow's serious affairs, so surely you will not have the heart to burn it. You will just have to find a little box and hide it away instead, which suits me perfectly.
No doubt you find that strange. With war at hand, and Khitans along the Hutuo River swarming like cockroaches, step on one and a whole nest comes scuttling out, how could there be nothing worth writing about?
Ah, but that is because I have lately come upon a secret so great it nearly rattled me apart. Truly, it is something astonishing.
But I am not telling you.
Serves you right for always saying my chatter spins like a cartwheel, turning and turning without ever reaching the point. Well then, I have learned my lesson. This time I shall say nothing at all. Heaven is high and the world is wide. You have no way of knowing beneath which eave I am prattling away at this very moment. Even if you stamp your foot in frustration, you still will not catch me. All you can do is stew.
I have always admired you. You can look after the Qi family estate, handle trade and the affairs of cultivation, and win the trust of so many besides. Even along the borderlands, the common folk often speak of you. Hearing it makes me proud, sweet as honey on the tongue.
But before long, my own name will be known throughout the realm as well. Once this business is done, the tales sung on the opera stage, the stories told in the teahouses, and the storybooks sold in every street and lane will all resound with Ding Xiang's great name.
Just you wait and see.

zh:
藏修斋者，枕山襟海之胜境也。其地负阴抱阳，左引青峦叠翠，右挹沧溟万里。斋依山势而筑，层阁叠起，若鸾凤栖云；海风自东来，涤荡尘嚣，清气满襟。昔为荒陬幽谷，今文脉生发，成天下庠序之冠。
学子分三科精研修业：文者究诗骚之旨，探六艺之微，每有佳构，辄刻于斋壁；史者钩沉竹帛，考镜得失，每论兴亡，常至夜分；法者明律令，析案例，设坛辩论，如廷诤然。三科虽异，而明理致用则一。尝有会讲之制，师儒高座，学子环侍，问难锋起，析理精微，乃杏坛盛事矣。
诸生朝夕砥砺，求圣贤之道。观其论《春秋》而明大义，析律典以拯黎元，吟风月而关乎治乱，岂非三代遗风乎？山岳可崩，而文心不朽，海潮有竭，而道脉长存。藏修之名，其意深矣——藏者，蓄德也；修者，进业也。白马之祸文脉俱断，于今再续，此乃文教之昌，基于斯斋乎？
en:
The Erudition Hall stands in a place of surpassing beauty, with mountains at its feet and the sea at its face. The land embraces both shadow and sunlight. To the left it draws in green peaks layered with verdure, to the right it takes in the vast expanse of the open sea. The hall is built along the momentum of the mountain, its tiered pavilions rising one upon another like a phoenix alighting among the clouds; the sea wind comes from the east, sweeping away the dust and clamor of the world, and fresh air fills one's robes. Though this place was once a desolate valley, today the cultural lineage has taken root and flourished here, and it has become the foremost crown of all academies under heaven.
Students specialize in three branches of study: Letters, which delves into the meaning of poetry and song, exploring the subtleties of the Six Arts—fine compositions are often carved upon the hall's walls; History, which unearths records from bamboo and silk, examining the rise and fall of dynasties, with debates on prosperity and decline often lasting past midnight; and Law, which clarifies statutes and analyzes cases, holding debates as formal as court proceedings. Though the three branches differ, all share the goal of illuminating principle for practical use. There was once a tradition of joint lectures, where esteemed scholars sat in honor while students gathered round, questions flying and arguments refined... Truly a grand occasion at the Apricot Altar.
The students strive day and night in pursuit of the sages' way. Watching them debate the Spring and Autumn Annals to grasp its great principles, analyze legal codes to save the common people, and compose verses on wind and moon that touch upon order and chaos. Is this not the legacy of the Three Dynasties? Mountains may crumble, yet the literary heart endures; the tides may ebb, yet the lineage of the Way persists. The name "Erudition Hall" carries deep meaning: to store is to accumulate virtue, to cultivate is to advance in learning. After the Baima Incident severed the cultural lineage entirely, it is here, in this very hall, that it has been rekindled. Is this not the flourishing of literary teaching?

zh:
【哀公问第二十七】

哀公问于孔子曰：“大礼何如？君子之言礼，何其尊也？”孔子曰：“丘也小人，不足以知礼。”君曰：“否！吾子言之也。”孔子曰：“丘闻之：民之所由生，礼为大。非礼无以节事天地之神也，非礼无以辨君臣上下长幼之位也，非礼无以别男女父子兄弟之亲、昏姻疏数之交也；君子以此之为尊敬然。然后以其所能教百姓，不废其会节。有成事，然后治其雕镂文章黼黻以嗣。其顺之，然后言其丧算，备其鼎俎，设其豕腊，修其宗庙，岁时以敬祭祀，以序宗族。即安其居，节丑其衣服，卑其宫室，车不雕几，器不刻镂，食不贰味，以与民同利。昔之君子之行礼者如此。”公曰：“今之君子胡莫行之也？”孔子曰：“今之君子，好实无厌，淫德不倦，荒怠傲慢，固民是尽，午其众以伐有道；求得当欲，不以其所。昔之用民者由前，今之用民者由后。今之君子莫为礼也。”
孔子侍坐于哀公，哀公曰：“敢问人道谁为大？”孔子愀然作色而对曰：“君之及此言也，百姓之德也！固臣敢无辞而对？人道，政为大。”公曰：“敢问何谓为政？”孔子对曰：“政者正也。君为正，则百姓从政矣。君之所为，百姓之所从也。君所不为，百姓何从？”公曰：“敢问为政如之何？”孔子对曰：“夫妇别，父子亲，君臣严。三者正，则庶物从之矣。”公曰：“寡人虽无似也，愿闻所以行三言之道，可得闻乎？”孔子对曰：“古之为政，爱人为大；所以治爱人，礼为大；所以治礼，敬为大；敬之至矣，大昏为大。大昏至矣！大昏既至，冕而亲迎，亲之也。亲之也者，亲之也。是故，君子兴敬为亲；舍敬，是遗亲也。弗爱不亲；弗敬不正。爱与敬，其政之本与！”
……
en:
【Duke Ai's Questions, Chapter 27】

Duke Ai asked Confucius, "What is the nature of the great rites? Why do gentlemen speak of rites with such reverence?" Confucius replied, "I am but a humble man and not worthy to understand the rites." The Duke said, "No! You must speak of them." Confucius said, "I have heard that among the means by which the people live, the rites are paramount. Without rites, one cannot regulate the services to the spirits of heaven and earth; without rites, one cannot distinguish the positions of ruler and minister, superior and inferior, elder and younger; without rites, one cannot differentiate the bonds between man and woman, father and son, elder and younger brother, nor the degrees of closeness in marriage and social intercourse. It is for this reason that gentlemen hold them in such high esteem. Then, with their abilities, they teach the common people, never neglecting the proper observances and seasons. When achievements are accomplished, they then attend to the carved ornaments, patterned embroidery, and ceremonial regalia to continue the tradition. When the people comply, they then set forth the mourning regulations, prepare the sacrificial vessels and stands, arrange the offerings of pork and dried meat, maintain the ancestral temples, and at the proper times of the year offer reverent sacrifices, thereby ordering the clan. They settle peacefully in their dwellings, keep their clothing modest, make their houses lowly, do not ornament their carriages, do not engrave their vessels, and do not seek variety in their food, so as to share benefits with the people. Such was the practice of gentlemen of old in performing the rites." The Duke said, "Why do the gentlemen of today not practice them?" Confucius said, "The gentlemen of today delight in possessions without satiety, indulge in excess without weariness, are idle and negligent, arrogant and rude, exhaust the people completely, and turn their multitudes against the righteous way; they seek to satisfy their desires without regard for what is proper. Those who employed the people in former times followed the former path; those who employ the people today follow the latter path. The gentlemen of today do not practice the rites."
Confucius was seated in attendance upon Duke Ai, and Duke Ai said, "May I ask what is greatest among the ways of man?" Confucius, with a solemn expression, replied, "That Your Lordship has spoken of this is a blessing to the common people! How dare I, your servant, answer without due consideration? Among the ways of man, governance is greatest." The Duke said, "May I ask what is meant by governance?" Confucius replied, "Governance means correctness. If the ruler is correct, then the common people will follow his governance. What the ruler does, the people follow. What the ruler does not do, how can the people follow?" The Duke said, "May I ask how one should practice governance?" Confucius replied, "Let husband and wife be distinguished, father and son be affectionate, and ruler and minister be strict. When these three are correct, all other matters will follow accordingly." The Duke said, "Though I am unworthy, I wish to hear the way to practice these three principles. May I hear it?" Confucius replied, "In governance of old, loving the people was paramount; in managing the love of people, the rites were paramount; in managing the rites, reverence was paramount; and at the height of reverence, the great marriage ceremony was paramount. The great marriage is the utmost! When the great marriage comes, the groom, in ceremonial cap, personally welcomes the bride—this is to show affection for her. Showing affection for her means treating her as kin. Therefore, the gentleman cultivates reverence to achieve intimacy; if reverence is abandoned, then kinship is lost. Without love, there is no intimacy; without reverence, there is no correctness. Love and reverence—are these not the very foundation of governance?"

zh:
顾穿扬是临安学府的骑射教习，长得那叫一个五大三粗，臂力也十分惊人。学生们不理解，这样的一位老师，怎么总是生病呢？ 
在学生们不知道的角落，顾穿扬叹了口气，他看着自己手中三张字迹不一，但写着同一句话的纸：
“老顾，我上。”
行吧，看来今天又无课可上了。
原本他也不是这般人尽可欺的，自从一位夫子去青州游历回来后，临安学府就变了天。
那些夫子喊着：
“我吴越儿郎不能输！”
“天下闻名的文津馆都这样做了，我们也不能落后！”
“他们的骑射老师总是身体有恙，为了学生们的未来，让老顾也身体抱恙吧！”
没课上的顾穿扬只好在学府附近的湖心亭溜达，和下棋的大爷们混成了忘年交。久而久之，棋艺倒是涨了不少，也逐渐爱上了下棋。
就在他于棋盘上杀个爽快之时，一名学生突然在他身旁冒头。
“顾先生！您怎么在这儿？”
“咳咳……旧疾又犯了呀，出来透透气。”
“吴夫子不是说您崴了脚吗？”
顾穿扬只能拼命咳嗽来掩盖自己的尴尬，一旁的大爷憋着笑说道：“穿扬啊，个么换个说法呀，侬这旧疾都犯八百回了。”
en:
Gu Chuanyang teaches mounted archery at Lin'an Academy. He's a hulking man with astonishingly powerful arms. His students can't understand it: how can someone built like that be sick all the time? 
Away from his students, Gu Chuanyang sighed over the three notes he was holding. The handwriting differed, but the message was the same:
"Gu, I'll take your class."
Right. No classes for him again today.
He hadn't always been such a pushover. But after one of the teachers returned from a trip to Qingzhou, everything changed at Lin'an Academy.
The teachers took up the cry:
"Our Wuyue boys won't be outdone!"
"Even the renowned Inkbound Order does it! We can't afford to fall behind!"
"Their mounted archery instructor is always sick. For our students' sake, Gu will just have to be sick too!"
With no classes to teach, Gu Chuanyang took to wandering down to the pavilion on the lake near the academy. He became fast friends with the old men who played there. Over time, his own game improved, and he grew to love it.
As he gleefully battled it out on the board, a student suddenly popped up beside him.
"Master Gu! What are you doing here?"
"Ahem... My old ailment's acting up again. Just getting some air."
"Didn't Master Wu say you'd sprained your ankle?"
Gu Chuanyang could only cough harder to cover his embarrassment. Beside him, one of the old men struggled to keep a straight face. "Chuanyang, you'll need a new excuse. That old ailment's flared up more times than I can count."

zh:
有一哑婆售卖“美人烛”，烛体晶莹，燃时甜香醉人。传言此烛油采自未嫁夭亡的少女之骨，燃之可见心中所想。
浪荡儿买回一支，闭门点燃。香气氤氲中，烛光摇曳，竟映出他朝思暮想的邻家女身影，巧笑倩兮，伸手邀他共舞。浪儿痴迷，日夜凝视，不吃不喝。三日后，甜香渐腐，烛光里的“美人”皮肉开始剥落，露出森森白骨，眼窝黑洞洞盯着他笑。浪荡儿惊觉想逃，双腿却如灌了蜡，动弹不得。烛火猛地一跳，那白骨美人倏地扑出烛焰，冰凉骨爪扼住他咽喉。
村中里正闻异臭破门，只见浪荡儿僵坐椅上，双目圆睁，嘴角凝固着一丝诡异痴笑。桌上烛已燃尽，只余一滩浑浊油脂，散发着甜腻与尸臭。烛泪蜿蜒，在他脚边凝成两个扭曲小字——“同归”。
那位邻家女早已于三日前死去，死前曾有贼人破门。后众人为其下葬时，发现脊骨少了一节。
en:
A mute old woman sold candles she called "Maiden's Candles." The wax was pale and translucent, and when lit, they gave off a sweet, heady fragrance. Rumor had it the tallow was rendered from the bones of girls who had died unwed. Light one, they said, and you would see whatever your heart most desired.
A wayward young man bought one, bolted his door, and put it to flame. Through the sweet-scented haze and the wavering light, the figure of the neighbor girl he had long pined for took shape. She smiled, dimples and all, and reached out her hand as if to draw him into a dance. He sat transfixed, day and night, forsaking food and drink.
On the third day, the sweetness curdled. The girl's form began to rot. Her flesh peeled away before his eyes, baring white bones that stared back at him with hollow sockets and a grinning jaw. He lurched to flee, but his legs were dead weight, heavy as poured wax. Then the flame lurched. The skeleton lunged from the fire, ice-cold bone fingers closing around his throat.

The village elder broke in when the smell became unbearable. He found the young man rigid in his chair, eyes wide open, a strange fixed smile on his face. The candle had burned to nothing, leaving a pool of cloudy grease on the table, sweet rot heavy in the air. Candle drippings had traced a path down to the floor, cooling into three twisted characters: "Come With Me."
The neighbor girl had died three days before, during a break-in. When the village buried her, they found one vertebra missing from her spine.

zh:
今日是苏家老夫人七十寿辰，苏府上下铺红结彩，宾客满席，喜气盈天。熙熙攘攘的客席之间，徐州各家名门的艳羡之声不绝于耳。
众人皆在讨论，这苏府不知从何处得了机缘，竟能搭上那传言中不见首亦不见尾的龙王？只是稍借那龙漕帮之势，经掌了一小程盐运，便是一飞冲天，将他们这些郡县豪族远远甩在了身后。
苏府主家老爷已五十岁，仍未去纨绔之气，他万未想到，苏家能在他之手得以中兴。今日老夫人寿辰，甫一开宴，他便喝得满面红光，目眩神迷。苏家老夫人剜了一眼不成器的儿子，而后看向如今真正当家做主的孙女苏婉，方和缓了神色。只是她的目光甫一触到苏婉身边那外姓人，便如遇蛇蝎，脸上尽是毫不遮掩的嫌恶之色。
“龙云天，今日宴上，苏婉自有她的事情要处置。苏府大事，你一外姓人不必知道，回厢房暂避就是！”
却说那龙云天，剑眉星目，面容瘦削，天然便带一股冷意。今日头发未得打理，随意束起，更带了几分江湖气。这样的男子，听闻大庭广众此等折辱之言，竟未做一声。他即是苏家赘婿，外人皆称，他将成苏婉一生之败笔。
龙云天望向苏婉，昔日百般不入苏老夫人之眼的女流之辈，如今尽得苏家权柄与敬爱的苏家主事，他的那位妻子。她如毫无所闻，仍言笑晏晏，与徐州别驾那私生子罗逢相谈甚欢。苏婉已尽数忘了，她被苏家逐出府去的落魄之时，是谁与她同舟共济。又是谁甘愿背赘婿之名，入府助她掌家族之权。
龙云天抬起眸子，恢复了些昔日的气度，他望向那高座之上的苏老夫人，言语之间尽是讥讽：“老夫人，你这是要给你家孙女，介绍一个私生子夫婿？我龙某是赘婿不假，却也不是死了！”
一时之间，满座哗然。
苏婉立马回身，怒目望向龙云天。望着宾客议论声起，苏婉强压怒气，冷冷劝慰：“夫君何出此言？你为赘婿，老夫人令你回避也无碍古礼。你怎可信口胡言，于这寿宴之上顶撞她老人家？”
“古礼……古礼？哈哈哈哈哈，好一个古礼！你可还记得，你被这老妖婆以女流之辈不得介入家业为由，逐出府外之时，是谁接济于你，甘愿以赘婿之名入苏府，与你共抗这古礼？”
苏老夫人大惊，怒指龙云天，恨不得当场要左右拿其性命：“狂悖之徒！狂悖之徒！我与婉婉皆是苏家人，前尘旧事，心结已解。如今婉婉治理家业，我苏家将成世家，你一外人，竟如此挑拨离间？”
苏老夫人望向苏婉，见苏婉亦现愠怒之色，终于安下心来。
“我与祖奶为一家，血浓于水，其又为长辈，你安敢作此不肖之言？看来我苏婉确实有眼无珠，你若要离府，我便遂你心意！来人，备纸墨，今日我苏婉，便在诸位名门见证之下，休了这不肖狂悖之徒！从此我苏婉，与这龙云天，再无瓜葛！”

龙云天怔怔无言，落下两行清泪。席中之人，有叹息之声，亦有哂笑之声，皆已不入云天之耳。那罗逢更是喜形于色，再不掩饰，望向苏婉的眼中尽是贪婪之色。
“苏州州牧遣使来贺！”
闻听门吏此言，更是满座哗然。苏老夫人与苏婉脸上的愠色一扫而空，就连那早已醉倒多时的苏府老爷都惊醒过来。
“哈哈哈哈，我就知道我苏府假以时日，必能成世家之族！”
“那龙某人！我女儿已休了你，你还在此处作甚？那罗家的私生之子，收起你那觊觎之心！我女儿岂是你能染指？须是州牧之嫡子，方配得上！”
苏婉皱眉，却也听得心下欢喜。州牧嫡子，那该是何等翩翩君子，英姿少年。再望向那形容邋遢，只是依附在他苏府的赘婿龙云天，心下厌恶更甚。好在，她苏婉终于能摆脱这无用之人了。
龙云天心下黯然，当此之时，那州牧使者恰望向此处，心下大惊。趋步上前，纳头便拜：
“昔日龙漕帮飞火营曹园，拜见龙王！”
众人尽皆瞠目！而苏婉终究灵慧，先一步反应过来，腿一软，当即瘫倒在地：“夫……夫君……”
但此次，再无那次星夜之下的俊朗少年将她扶起，龙云天未往此处多看一眼。他只是将曹园搀起，上下打量后，认出来人，笑道：
”竟长这么大了。州牧府中待你如何，他若亏待了你，我可不饶他。“
”一切皆好。州牧听到你隐去身份藏在这苏府的密报，本想亲自前来一见，奈何事务繁忙抽不出身。又闻龙卫称，你并不愿暴露身份，便只遣了我来。只是未想到，龙王之身，竟被这小小苏府折辱！“
老夫人脸色灰白，赶忙自主位趋步而来。金冠太重，华服太长，竟跌了一跤，但她仍半刻不敢歇，手脚并用向龙云天爬来。
龙云天冷哼一声，当今圣驾亦曾与他把酒言欢，今至苏府，竟被折辱至此。
他再不回头看那狼狈丑恶的老夫人，亦不看那被吓得连连磕头的苏府老爷，更不看那瘫倒在地的苏婉。
这些都是我给苏府的，今我离去，便尽数收回吧。从此后，苏家如何没落，与他再不相干！
再无苏家赘婿，只有龙漕龙王！
en:
Today marks the seventieth birthday of Matriarch Su. The entire Homestead is draped in festive crimson, a sea of lanterns and silks radiating joy to the heavens.
Guests huddle in hushed conversation: how did the Sus, of all people, secure the favor of the Dragon King of the Dragon Tide Clan? Word on the street is that by riding the coattails of the Dragon Tide Clan, they've seized a portion of the salt trade. That single move sent them soaring, leaving Xuzhou's local gentry scrambling in their wake.
Patriarch Su, a man of fifty who has yet to outgrow his hedonistic streaks, is lost in a drunken haze, his face flushed with the pride of a family reborn. The Matriarch shoots a scathing look at her useless son and then turns to her granddaughter, Su Wan, the true power behind the family. Only then does her gaze soften. But as her eyes drift to the outsider standing beside Su Wan, they narrow with venomous spite.
"Long Yuntian, Su Wan has serious matters to attend to. No place for an outsider. Withdraw to the guest wing now!"
This Long Yuntian possesses a sharp, ascetic face with eyes like distant stars, radiating a natural, frigid aura. His unkempt hair, bound loosely today, lends him an air of the wild, untamed jianghu. Despite the public humiliation, he remains silent. He is the matrilocal groom of the Sus. To the world, he is the greatest blemish on Su Wan's otherwise perfect life.
Long Yuntian's gaze falls on Su Wan, the woman who has once been cast aside by the matriarch but now stands at the center of power, the de facto head of the Su family. She acts as if he didn't exist, her face bright with charm as she shares a laugh with Luo Feng, the illegitimate son of the Vice-Governor, as if she'd completely forgotten who stood by her when she was thrown out of the Su Homestead in disgrace, who willingly took on the humiliating label of the matrilocal groom just so she could reclaim control of the family.
Long Yuntian raises his head, the suppressed dignity of his past resurfacing. His voice drips with cold irony: "Tell me, Matriarch, is this your plan? To pimp out your granddaughter to a bastard? I'm still Su Wan's husband, whether you like it or not."
A ripple of shock and murmurs sweeps through the hall.
Su Wan spins around, her eyes blazing as they lock onto Long Yuntian. Sensing the guests' prying eyes, Su Wan suppresses her fury. "Enough! For a matrilocal groom, obeying the Matriarch is the highest propriety. How dare you hurl such reckless insults on her very birthday?"
"Propriety? Ha! A fine word for it! Do you forget, Su Wan? When that old crone cast you out, claiming a woman had no place in the family business, who stood by you? Who took the brand of the 'matrilocal groom' just to fight that very 'propriety' by your side?"
The Matriarch trembles, her finger jabbing the air at him. "You insolent cur! Wan and I are of one blood; the past is buried. Now that she leads our house to greatness, how dare you, a mere outsider, to sow discord?"
The Matriarch glances at Su Wan and, seeing the anger flash across her granddaughter's face, finally relaxes.
"Blood is thicker than your lies. How dare you spout such filth against your elders? Bring paper and ink! Today, before all the honored guests, I, Su Wan, sever our ties. We're done from this day forth!"

Long Yuntian stands frozen, tears silently streaming down his face. The crowd buzzes, some sighing, others sneering, but the noise barely registers. Luo Feng can barely contain his glee. He no longer hides the hunger in his eyes as he leers at Su Wan.
"Greetings from the Suzhou Governor!"
At that announcement, the hall stirs again. The Matriarch and Su Wan quickly smooth over their expressions. Even the Patriarch, who's been half-dead drunk moments ago, jolts awake.
"Hahaha! I knew it! The Su name was destined for the halls of the Great Clans!"
"You! Long Yuntian! My daughter has cast you off. Why are you still here? And you, Luo's bastard, tuck away your pathetic lust! My girl is no prize for the likes of you. Only the Governor's firstborn is worthy!"
Su Wan frowns but feels a secret thrill. The Governor's firstborn... He must be a paragon of grace, a hero among men. She spares a glance at Long Yuntian, unkempt, a mere parasite clinging to her family's shadow. Her disgust curdles in her throat. Finally, she'll be free of this useless man.
Long Yuntian's gaze remains cold and distant. But as the Governor's envoy scans the room, his eyes lock onto Long, and his blood runs cold. He scrambles forward and throws himself to the floor in a frantic kowtow.
"Cao Yuan, formerly of the Flying Fire Battalion, Dragon Tide Clan, pays humble homage to the Dragon King!"
The entire hall is frozen in collective shock. But Su Wan, ever the pragmatist, is the first to grasp the gravity. Her knees buckle, and she collapses in a heap. "Hus... Husband..."
But this time, Long is no longer that considerate youth. He does not spare her even a fleeting glance. Instead, he helps Cao Yuan up, studying the man's features until recognition clicks. He offers a rare smile.
"You've grown quite a bit, haven't you? How does the Governor treat you? If he's shown you any slight, he'll have me to answer to."
"All's well. The Governor received word of your seclusion here. He intended to pay his respects in person, but the burdens of his office held him back. Hearing from the Dragon Guard that you wished to keep your identity hidden, he sent me instead. Little did we expect that the great Dragon King would be subjected to such indignity by this... pathetic Su clan!"
The Matriarch's face turns a deathly gray. She scrambles from her seat of honor in a blind panic. Her golden crown is too heavy, her silk robes too cumbersome; she trips and falls, yet she does not stop. She crawls toward him on all fours, a desperate, broken creature.
Long lets out a sharp, cold snort. He was once a favored guest at the emperor's table, yet here, in this house, he was treated as filth.
He casts not a single look back at the wretched crone, nor the trembling Lord Su, who thumps his head against the floor in mindless terror. Not even at Su Wan, broken and silent on the ground.
"Everything the Su family possesses was my gift. Now that I depart, I reclaim it all. From this moment on, the ruin of the Sus is of no consequence to me."
The matrilocal groom is gone. Only the Dragon King of the Dragon Tide Clan!

zh:
阿笙是叱咤江湖的武林世家的家主。外头都传，他孤傲冷漠，不善与人相交。但那日他拉住我时，却极为温柔。他还告诉我，他的爷爷病入膏肓，唯一的心愿便是能看到他成家。但他们在武林中享有盛名，外头的女子都心怀鬼胎。唯有眼下一无所有的我，是他最好的选择。阿笙还说，他醉心武学，对男女情爱并无兴趣。若我愿意嫁给他，我可以选一处清净的园子，做我想做的任何事情。那日他絮絮叨叨的，在我面前说了许多话，像是唯恐我拒绝。
但我没有拒绝的理由。
眼下我一无所有，没了上官家小娘子的身份，我在这世道根本无法存活。最重要的是，阿笙，阿笙，这个名字，我曾在无数个日夜反反复复地念起。是了，他从很早之前，便是我藏在心间，不敢提及的人……
我在半个月后嫁给了阿笙。婚后，我搬进了一处安静的院子里。阿笙偶尔会来看我，但更多的时候，他履行着他的承诺，离我远远的，唯恐打扰了我。而我也安于这般的现状。我知道，他娶我，半是出于对爷爷的交代，另一半，不过是同情我的遭遇。他对我并无情意。而眼下的我，也没有资格再去苛求一段感情。
但三个月后，在阿笙的生日宴后，我却知道了一个惊人的秘密……
en:
A'Sheng was the head of a prestigious martial family, a man who commanded great respect across the jianghu. People say he was proud and cold, ill at ease with human interactions. But the day he reached out and caught me, his touch was unbearably gentle. He told me that his grandfather was gravely ill, and that his only wish was to see A'Sheng married. In the martial world, fame brought suspicion, and every woman who approached them had ulterior motives. Only someone like me, stripped of all status and possessions, was his best choice. A'Sheng added that he cared little for love, his heart was devoted to martial arts alone. If I agreed to marry him, I could choose a quiet garden for myself and live as I pleased. That day, he spoke at length, endlessly,
as if terrified that I might refuse.

But I had no reason to refuse.

I had nothing left. Without my title as the Shangguan family's daughter, I could not survive in this world. And most importantly, A'Sheng. I had whispered to myself his name through countless nights, the one I had long buried in my heart, too afraid to ever speak out.

Half a month later, I became his wife. After the wedding, I moved into a quiet courtyard. A'Sheng would visit me from time to time, but more often, he kept his distance, honoring his promise not to disturb me. And I accepted this arrangement. I knew he had married me partly to fulfill his grandfather's wish, and partly out of sympathy for my fall from grace. There was no love between us. And as I was then, I had no right to demand love from anyone.

But three months later, after A'Sheng's birthday banquet, I discovered a shocking secret...

zh:
【曾子问第七】

曾子问曰：“君薨而世子生，如之何？”孔子曰：“卿、大夫、士从摄主，北面于西阶南。大祝裨冕，执束帛，升自西阶，尽等，不升堂，命毋哭。祝声三，告曰：‘某之子生，敢告。’升，奠币于殡东几上，哭降。众主人、卿、大夫、士、房中皆哭，不踊，尽一哀，反位，遂朝奠。小宰升，举币。三日，众主人、卿、大夫、士如初位，北面，大宰、大宗、大祝皆裨冕，少师奉子以衰，祝先，子从，宰、宗人从，入门，哭者止。子升自西阶，殡前北面，祝立于殡东南隅。祝声三，曰：‘某之子某，从执事，敢见。’子拜稽颡，哭，祝、宰、宗人、众主人、卿、大夫、士哭，踊三者三，降，东反位，皆祖。子踊，房中亦踊，三者三，袭，衰，杖，奠出。大宰命祝、史，以名徧告于五祀、山川。”曾子问曰：“如已葬而世子生，则如之何？”孔子曰：“大宰、大宗从大祝而告于祢。三月，乃名于祢，以名徧告及，社稷、宗庙、山川。”
孔子曰：“诸侯适天子，必告于祖，奠于祢，冕而出视朝。命祝、史告于社稷、宗庙、山川，乃命国家五官而后行，道而出。告者五日而徧，过是非礼也。凡告用牲、币，反亦如之。诸侯相见，必告于祢，朝服而出视朝。命祝、史告于五庙，所过山川，亦命国家五官，道而出。反必亲告于祖、祢，乃命祝、史告至于前所告者，而后听朝而入。”
曾子问曰：“并有丧，如之何？何先何后？”孔子曰：“葬，先轻而后重；其奠也，先重而后轻，礼也。自启及葬不奠，行葬不哀次，反葬奠，而后辞于殡，遂修葬事。其虞也，先重而后轻，礼也。”孔子曰：“宗子虽七十，无无主妇；非宗子，虽无主妇可也。”
曾子问曰：“将冠子，冠者至，揖让而入，闻齐衰、大功之丧，如之何？”孔子曰：“内丧则废。外丧则冠而不醴，彻馔而埽，即位而哭。如冠者未至，则废。如将冠子而未及期日，而有齐衰、大功、小功之丧，则因丧服而冠。”“除丧不改冠乎？”孔子曰：“天子赐诸侯、大夫冕、弁服于大庙，归设奠，服赐服，于斯乎有冠醮，无冠醴。父没而冠，则巳冠埽地而登于祢，巳祭而见伯父、叔父，而后飨冠者。”
曾子问曰：“祭如之何则不行旅酬之事矣？”孔子曰：“闻之，小祥者，主人练祭而不旅，奠酬于宾，宾弗举，礼也。昔者鲁昭公练而举酬行旅，非礼也；孝公大祥，奠酬弗举，亦非礼也。”
曾子问曰：“大功之丧，可以与于馈奠之事乎？”孔子曰：“岂大功耳，自斩衰以下皆可，礼也。”曾子曰：“不以轻服而重相为乎？”孔子曰：“非此之谓也。天子、诸侯之丧，斩衰者奠；大夫齐衰者奠，士则朋友奠。不足则取于大功以下者，不足则反之。”曾子问曰：“小功可以与于祭乎？”孔子曰：“何必小功耳，自斩衰以下与祭，礼也。”曾子曰：“不以轻丧而重祭乎？”孔子曰：“天子、诸侯之丧祭也，不斩衰者不与祭。大夫齐衰者与祭。士祭不足，则取于兄弟大功以下者。”曾子问曰：“相识，有丧服，可以与于祭乎？”孔子曰：“缌不祭，又何助于人？”

en:
【Master Zeng's Questions, Chapter 7】

Master Zeng asked: "If a ruler dies and a legitimate son is born afterward, what should be done?" Confucius said: "The ministers, great officers, and officers follow the acting chief mourner, facing north at the south of the western steps. The Grand Prayer, in ceremonial robes and cap, holding a bundle of silk, ascends from the western steps, stops at the top step without entering the hall, and commands that no one weep. The Prayer calls out three times, announcing: 'A son has been born to so-and-so, I dare to report.' He ascends, places the silk offering on the table east of the coffin, weeps, and descends. The chief mourners, ministers, great officers, officers, and women in the chambers all weep without leaping, completing one period of mourning, then return to their positions and proceed with the morning offering. The Lesser Steward ascends and removes the silk. On the third day, the chief mourners, ministers, great officers, and officers take their positions as before, facing north. The Grand Steward, Grand Ancestral Officer, and Grand Prayer all wear ceremonial robes and caps. The Young Tutor presents the child wearing mourning garments. The Prayer goes first, the child follows, with the Steward and Ancestral Officer following behind. They enter the gate, and the weepers cease. The child ascends from the western steps, faces north before the coffin, while the Prayer stands at the southeast corner of the funeral chamber. The Prayer calls out three times, saying: 'The son of so-and-so, named such, following the attendants, dares to present himself.' The child kowtows, weeps, and the Prayer, Steward, Ancestral Officer, chief mourners, ministers, great officers, and officers weep, leaping three times in sets of three. They descend, return east to their positions, and all bare their arms. The child leaps, and the women in the chambers also leap, three times in sets of three. Then they put on their garments, mourning sashes, and staffs, and proceed with the offering before departing. The Grand Steward orders the Prayer and Recorder to announce the child's name to the five sacrifices and the mountains and rivers." Master Zeng asked: "If the ruler has already been buried when the legitimate son is born, what should be done?" Confucius said: "The Grand Steward and Grand Ancestral Officer follow the Grand Prayer to announce to the deceased father. After three months, the name is formally given at the father's shrine, and it is announced everywhere, including to the altars of soil and grain, ancestral temples, and mountains and rivers."
Confucius said: "When a feudal lord goes to visit the Son of Heaven, he must announce to his ancestors and offer sacrifice at his father's shrine, then put on his ceremonial cap and hold court. He orders the Prayer and Recorder to announce to the altars of soil and grain, ancestral temples, and mountains and rivers, then instructs the five officers of his state before departing, and sets out after performing the farewell sacrifice. The announcements should be completed within five days; exceeding this is contrary to ritual. All announcements use animals and silk, and upon return, the same is done. When feudal lords meet each other, they must announce at their father's shrine, put on court robes, and hold court. They order the Prayer and Recorder to announce to the five ancestral temples and the mountains and rivers they will pass, and also instruct the five officers of their state, then set out after the farewell sacrifice. Upon return, they must personally announce to their ancestors and father's shrine, then order the Prayer and Recorder to announce their arrival to those previously announced to, and only then attend court and enter."
Master Zeng asked: "If there are two simultaneous mourning obligations, what should be done? Which comes first and which comes last?" Confucius said: "For burial, the lighter mourning obligation comes first, then the heavier; for offerings, the heavier comes first, then the lighter—this is proper ritual. From the opening of the coffin chamber to the burial, no offerings are made; during the funeral procession, one does not stop at the mourning hut. After returning from burial, offerings are made, and then farewell is taken at the funeral chamber, after which burial matters are completed. For the repose sacrifice, the heavier mourning comes first, then the lighter—this is proper ritual." Confucius said: "Even if the eldest son of the main line is seventy years old, he must not lack a principal wife to manage the household; if he is not the eldest son of the main line, it is permissible to lack a principal wife."
Master Zeng asked: "If one is about to perform the capping ceremony for a son, and the guests have arrived and have been ushered in with bows, when news comes of a mourning obligation of the qi cui or da gong degree, what should be done?" Confucius said: "If the mourning is within the household, the ceremony is abandoned. If it is outside the household, the capping proceeds but without the sweet wine offering; the feast is cleared away and the place swept, then positions are taken and weeping begins. If the guests have not yet arrived, the ceremony is abandoned. If one is about to cap a son but before the appointed day arrives, and a mourning obligation of qi cui, da gong, or xiao gong occurs, then the capping is performed along with the mourning garments." "After the mourning period ends, is the capping not redone?" Confucius said: "When the Son of Heaven bestows upon a feudal lord or great officer the cap and robe of office at the Grand Temple, upon return they set up an offering, wear the bestowed garments, and at this point there is a capping with the wine toast but no sweet wine ceremony. If the father has died before the capping, then after the capping is completed, the ground is swept and one ascends to the father's shrine; after the sacrifice, one presents oneself to the paternal uncles, and only then feasts the capping guests."
Master Zeng asked: "In what kind of sacrifice is the ceremony of circulating the drinking cups not performed?" Confucius said: "I have heard that at the one-year memorial, the chief mourner performs the pure sacrifice without circulating the cups; the offering cup is presented to the guests, but the guests do not raise it—this is proper ritual. In the past, Duke Zhao of Lu, at the one-year memorial, raised the cups and circulated them, which was contrary to ritual; Duke Xiao, at the two-year memorial, presented the offering cup without raising it, which was also contrary to ritual."
Master Zeng asked: "Can one who is in da gong mourning participate in the presentation of offerings and funeral rites?" Confucius said: "Not only da gong—from zhan cui downward, all may participate; this is proper ritual." Master Zeng said: "Is this not treating light mourning garments lightly and heavy mutual assistance heavily?" Confucius said: "That is not what is meant. At the mourning of the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord, those in zhan cui make the offerings; at that of a great officer, those in qi cui make the offerings; at that of an officer, friends make the offerings. If there are not enough people, they are drawn from those in da gong or below; if still insufficient, the process is repeated." Master Zeng asked: "Can one in xiao gong mourning participate in the sacrifice?" Confucius said: "Why only xiao gong—from zhan cui downward, all may participate in the sacrifice; this is proper ritual." Master Zeng said: "Is this not treating light mourning lightly and sacrifice heavily?" Confucius said: "At the mourning sacrifices of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords, those not in zhan cui do not participate. At that of a great officer, those in qi cui participate. At that of an officer, if there are not enough participants for the sacrifice, they are drawn from brothers in da gong or below." Master Zeng asked: "If one knows the deceased and is in mourning garments, can one participate in the sacrifice?" Confucius said: "One in si mourning does not even offer sacrifice himself—how much less can he assist others?"

然形骸有尽，意气无穷。人之肝胆，岂为生死困？有民赵铁，子陷于城，虽锋镝塞途，犹数入危城，不顾念己身，此之为父不裂之肝胆也。

In early December of the third year of Kaiyun, the Khitan army bypassed the Western Hills to strike the Jin army's rear, severing their supply lines. A hundred elite cavalry launched a daring raid on Luancheng. Though defended by a thousand soldiers, the garrison capitulated in shameful disarray. With the city's populace at their mercy, the Khitans branded some of their faces with the words "Imperial Mercy," then drove them south to shatter the resolve of the realm.
Yet while the flesh is finite, the spirit knows no bounds. Shall a person's courage be trapped by the flimsy quilt of life and death? A commoner named Zhao Tie, his son trapped within Luancheng's walls, braved roads choked with steel to enter the doomed city time and again, without a thought for his own safety. This was a father's unbreakable resolve.

en:
In the first year of Qianyou, tribute was paid to Han: thirty-four thousand jin of tea, along with incense, medicine, and weaponry.
...
In the second year of Guangshun, tribute was paid to Zhou: imperial robes, rhinoceros-horn belts, gold-and-silver-adorned weaponry, gold and silver vessels, damask silk and thin silk, tea, incense, medicine, imperial celadon porcelain, saddles and clogs, seafood delicacies, wine, and more.
In the third year of Guangshun, tribute was paid to Zhou: twenty-eight thousand bolts of damask and thin silk, six thousand liang of silver vessels, fifty thousand liang of silk floss, thirty thousand and fifty jin of tea, along with two sets of imperial robes, a pierced rhinoceros-horn belt, a dragon-patterned gold belt, incense and medicine, porcelain wares, silver-adorned armor and weaponry, ceremonial wine, seafood delicacies, and more.
...
In the third year of Xiande, tribute was paid to Zhou: five thousand liang of silver, ten thousand bolts of damask, one thousand five hundred liang of gold-flowered silver vessels for the Tianqing Festival, along with an imperial robe with a gold belt, brocade and silk damask, and more.
In the second month of the fifth year of Xiande, tribute was paid to Zhou: imperial robes, rhinoceros-horn belts, damask and thin silk, white metal, incense and medicine, along with two hundred thousand shi of rice to supply the army.
In the fourth month, tribute was paid to Zhou: twenty thousand bolts each of damask and thin silk, ten thousand liang of silver.
In the intercalary seventh month, tribute was paid to Zhou: five thousand liang of silver, twenty thousand bolts of thin silk, three thousand liang of silver vessels, two thousand bundles of fine cloth segments, along with an imperial robe with a coiled-dragon rhinoceros-horn belt, and more.

zh:
尽管不理解，但冰魄魄还是认真地经营着自己的三个小家。
直到有一天深夜，它的房门被敲响了。
来者是一位香喷喷的大姐姐。踏着清辉而入，她发髻上挽着的金色小花熠熠生辉。
“我敲了很多间屋子，都没有回应。你是第一个回应我的人。”
“我是途径此地的旅者。深夜饥渴，能否，讨碗水喝？”
冰魄魄揉了揉眼睛，礼貌地把大姐姐让进屋。
拉开橱柜，冰魄魄发现这个家里的水粮早就没了。毕竟，自己来这里住的时间也不多。
她抱起坛子，冒冒失失地向来客道歉。
“对、对不起，家里没、没有水和吃的了。你等等，我这就去找！”
“你慢些……”来客温柔地微笑。
真奇怪，明明自己才是主人，可那位大姐姐端坐在椅子上，却有一股从容不迫的气度。

摸黑来到屋后的河边，冰魄魄不知道自己摔了几次。真奇怪，今晚的夜色浓的看不到路。
冰魄魄只好瞪大双眼，竖起耳朵，才勉强听得到河水的声音。她把水坛沉入河中。
突然，冰魄魄瞪大了眼睛——
因为它发现，原本倒映在水中的那轮明月，此刻已经消失不见。
抬起头，天幕中只剩下漆黑一片。万籁寂静，甚至群星都失去了声喉。
周围只剩下自己的心跳，还有潺潺的水声。冰魄魄大叫一声，急忙往家里跑去。
en:
Though she didn't fully understand, Ice Soul diligently managed her three little homes. 
Until one late night, her door was knocked upon. 
The visitor was a sweet-smelling elder sister. Stepping in on beams of light, the golden flower pinned in her hair shone brightly. 
"I knocked on many doors, but no one answered. You are the first to respond." 
"I am a traveler passing through. Thirsty and hungry late at night... might I trouble you for a bowl of water?" 
Ice Soul rubbed her eyes and politely invited the elder sister inside. 
Opening the cupboard, Ice Soul found this home's water and food long gone. After all, she hadn't stayed here much. 
Hugging the jar, she stammered an apology to the guest. 
"S-sorry, there's no water or food here. Please wait, I'll go find some!" 
"Take your time..." the guest smiled gently. 
It was strange. She was the host, yet the elder sister sitting on the chair carried an air of unshakable composure. 

Groping her way to the river behind the house in the dark, Ice Soul lost count of her falls. So strange—tonight's darkness was so thick she couldn't see the path. 
Ice Soul had to widen her eyes and prick her ears to barely hear the river's flow. She submerged the water jar. 
Suddenly, Ice Soul's eyes widened— 
Because she discovered the moon that should have been reflected in the water had vanished. 
Looking up, only blackness remained in the sky. Utter silence, even the stars had lost their voices. 
Only her own heartbeat and the murmuring water remained. Ice Soul cried out and hurried back home.

zh:
小八坚信，自己是个讨人喜欢的。

 只是张万师消失后，很少有人“懂”他的那些奇思妙想罢了。好在他小八不缺好运气：卧星岩就有一位颇有意思又十分懂行的云婆婆，不仅对他的机巧设计大为赞叹，更是能不拘常理、顺着他的思路点拨一番。 

可惜那位云婆婆老忘记他的名字，还总在畅谈后塞给他特殊质地的铁环，并且强调：“这环是婆婆从天上摘下来的，遇上很好的朋友才会送呢！”

 哎，云婆婆年迈，脑子已经不是很好使了。但是恰好，他的脑袋也不怎么好。他们一个记性不好，但是长命百岁；一个聪明绝顶，但是命不久矣，这简直……就是天生注定的朋友嘛！
 小八将自己这精妙的见解分享给了云婆婆，云婆婆哈哈大笑：“那可更得好好活，活得越久，朋友越多！”说着又给他塞了一枚铁环。

 随着铁环越积越多，小八真的拥有了很多朋友。因为云婆婆认识了陆婆婆，认识了梓苑，认识了好多好多人……

 哈哈，果然，小八就是很受欢迎的人！
en:
Xiaoba has always believed he is a very likable person. It's just that after Master Zhang vanished, hardly anyone really understood his wild ideas anymore.
Luckily, Xiaoba has never been short on good fortune. At Stellabed Rocks, there was Granny Yun, a delightfully unusual woman who truly knew her craft. She admired his ingenious designs and, instead of dismissing them, always seemed able to follow his thinking and offer exactly the right insight.
The only problem was that Granny Yun could never seem to remember his name. Every time they had a good long talk, she would press another iron ring of some strange metal into his hand and say, "I picked this ring from the sky. I only give them to very good friends."
Well, Granny Yun was old, and her memory was not what it used to be. Then again, Xiaoba's head was not entirely right either. One of them was forgetful but likely to live to a hundred, while the other was brilliant but did not have long to live. Really, what could that make them but friends by fate?
When Xiaoba shared this brilliant conclusion with Granny Yun, she burst out laughing. "Then you'd better live well. The longer you live, the more friends you'll have." And with that, she tucked yet another iron ring into his hand.
As the rings piled up, Xiaoba truly did end up with many friends. Through Granny Yun, he came to know Granny Lu, Zi Yuan, and so many others besides.
Ha, just as he thought. Xiaoba really was the kind of person everyone liked.

zh:
贺家先祖贺怀智曾为唐玄宗时梨园乐师，为坐部伎之首，擅琵琶。安史之乱后，贺家来到湖州隐居，务农为生，日趋保守，贺怀智传下的石琵琶便被封入地窖，再无人问津，直到年幼的贺家长子发现了它。

这贺家长子自幼就叛逆，不爱诗书，偏爱戏文，偏爱一句“一笑万古春，一啼万古愁”，便抛去了父母之名，令众人以“万春”称呼自己。他见这琵琶陈旧古怪，十分好奇，便伸手拨弄，谁知这琵琶弦不知为何种金属所制，坚韧无比，贺万春年幼力轻，竟弹之不动，这却激起了贺万春的好胜心。他日日暗中潜入地窖，用尽力气拨弄这琵琶，终于在数日之后，偶然将其中最细一根琵琶弦撼动，弦音袅袅，不绝于耳，较之普通琴音深厚弥久，贺万春闻之心驰动摇，只觉得这乐音竟比听过的所有声响都好听。他日日流连在地窖深处拨弄石琵琶，不知不觉竟能将五根弦全部弹动，于是欣喜异常，便尽兴乱弹一番，谁知此泛音竟穿透地窖层层石壁，惊动村中众人。时值贺家服丧期间，保守的贺父因万春的顽劣而怒不可遏，当即令人将那石琵琶砸毁，谁知这琵琶身坚硬无比，无论石砸火烧，皆不能损其分毫。贺父便索性将它丢入村外山崖下，以此断了儿子习乐的念头。谁知贺万春竟因此大病一场，族中便有传言，此子莫非是琵琶成精，流言蜚语层出不穷，贺父不堪其扰，与万春日益疏远，万春亦是日日低落，就连自小圆滚滚的身子也瘦了一大圈。

后来机缘巧合，一个戏班进村表演，贺万春前去看戏，竟觉得与这些人越聊越是投机，想到自己在家中、族中、村中都无人重视，倒不如和这些人一同闯荡，于是两袖一甩，离家出走，随着戏班闯天涯去了。

后来一次未央城的斗艺会上，一位教坊主人亮出了一把唐代的琵琶，那琵琶通体石制，贺万春一眼便认出了那是自家的琵琶。他当场指出，希望教坊主人归还，可教坊主人亦是重金收购，岂愿割爱？二人争执时，一三十余岁的男子飘然现身，笑说石琵琶之主自然能够弹奏此物，既然二人都称是这琵琶的主人，不如各自演奏一曲作为证明。教坊主自诩擅长琵琶，便率先弹奏，谁知那石琵琶沉重无比，他抱不起来，只得倚靠琵琶弹奏，而琴弦却又坚韧生硬，不仅无法弹动还割破了他的手指。贺万春大笑，上前将琵琶扛起，抵在肩头，伸手在琵琶弦上一顿挥舞，弦音阵阵，可传万里，只是音调紊乱，不能成曲。那教坊主丢了脸，大为愤怒，便令坊中众人将石琵琶夺回，更要将贺万春双手打断。贺万春自然不甘示弱，但他双拳难敌四手，正要被磋磨时，先前那三十余岁的男子却出手将他护住，更现出身份，原来他便是梨园代园主胡昌翼。

胡昌翼花钱买下琵琶，告诉贺万春，若想得到琵琶，便和自己回梨园去，贺万春只得答应。进到梨园，贺万春先是习乐，谁知他先将舫内的琵琶弦弹断三百根，又将羯鼓敲破五十面，泣露舫内笛、筝、阮咸、排箫、羯鼓、筚篥、竽、方响、琵琶、拍板等乐器皆被他祸害了个遍，最终泣露舫司乐忍无可忍，认为此子并无习乐天分，遂将贺万春转入回雪舫。贺万春入回雪舫后，与小部弟子一同习歌舞，但他五音不全，一张嘴便将整首曲子的韵律尽数搅乱，几次三番后韶舞便令他只学群舞。但贺万春筋骨坚韧，舞蹈时全无“飘然回雪”之态，且长手长脚，孔武有力，挪腾时常不慎牵连周遭舞伴，最终不过在剑舞、字舞上勉强有些成果，除此之外令众师兄弟避之唯恐不及。回雪舫韶舞认为此子亦无歌舞天分，见贺万春倒是有一身好力气，便留他在各部间做些搬运乐器、布置戏台的事务。

贺万春不免心下愤懑，心想既然如此还不如回去与戏班子一起四处流浪。于是在夜间抱着那石琵琶在湖畔弹奏，将一腔抑郁无奈尽数倾泻于琵琶声中。他弹奏得起劲，却不知那石琵琶声响远比普通琵琶更加强劲，弦音在湖面扩散，竟吵得整个梨园上下不得安睡，也惊动了在琴风亭饮酒的胡昌翼。胡昌翼寻声找到贺万春，得知他学艺以来的经历，不禁讶异，他考较贺万春一番，发现他手指纤长有力，兼之听力过人、记心甚好，正是弹奏乐器的好材料，怎会被泣露舫断定不适合习乐？直至了解到贺万春在泣露舫的种种行为举止，这才明白过来：贺万春弹奏的石琵琶是贺怀智所制，琵琶身沉重异常，琵琶弦坚韧无比，贺万春小小年纪以此乐器为启蒙，导致他无法掌握弹奏乐器的力道，反倒耽误了他的才华。

自此之后，胡昌翼便令贺万春重回泣露舫，但他演奏乐器时须得手握鸡卵，若卵碎则表示力道过大，何时可手握鸡卵完整弹完一曲，便可正式习乐，此前不可再弹奏石琵琶。此后足足过了一年，贺万春方能做到令鸡卵不碎而弹完一曲。那之后便进展奇快，将泣露舫诸般乐器、乐谱学遍。待他能够操演寻常诸般乐器后，胡昌翼又将石琵琶还予他，令贺万春再次以此为乐器，演奏时依旧手握鸡卵。直至三年后，贺万春可手握鸡卵弹奏石琵琶，一曲尽而鸡卵不碎，胡昌翼方算他出师。此时贺万春一手琵琶技艺已为泣露舫坐部伎之首。

贺万春是个坐不住的，与园主打了招呼，便时常外出游历，渐渐地，贺万春的声名传闻江湖，人称梨园“六大名伶”之一。
en:
He family's ancestor, He Huaizhi, was an excellent pipa player who led the seated musical division in Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's Masked Troupe Orchestra. After the An Lushan Rebellion, the He family went into seclusion in Huzhou, turning to farming as they grew increasingly conservative. He Huaizhi's stone pipa was sealed in a cellar, forgotten until the eldest son of the He family discovered it.

The son had rebelled against tradition since childhood. Disdaining poetry and classics, he obsessed over operatic tales and the line, "A smile brings eternal spring, a tear invokes endless sorrow." He cast off his given name, insisting everyone call him "Wanchun". Intrigued by the pipa's peculiar aged appearance, he struggled to pluck at its strings, only to find them made of an unknown and impossibly tough metal. Despite being too weak to play a single note, he grew determined. Sneaking into the cellar daily, he strained to play until, after days of effort, he accidentally vibrated the thinnest string. Its melody lingered, deeper and more resonant than any he'd heard, captivating him utterly. Soon, he could play all five strings. He played recklessly, unaware the harmonics pierced the cellar walls and startled the village. During the family's mourning period, his conservative father flew into a rage, ordering the pipa smashed. But its body resisted rocks and fire alike, so he threw it off a cliff outside the village to curb his son's musical obsession. Wanchun fell gravely ill, fueling rumors that he was a pipa spirit in human form. His father grew distant, and Wanchun withered, losing his childhood plumpness.

By some twist of fate, an opera troupe came to perform in the village. When Wanchun went to watch, he found himself increasingly drawn to the performers during their conversations. Realizing he was overlooked and unappreciated at home, within the clan, and in the village, he decided it was better to strike out with the troupe. With a flick of his sleeves, he left home and wandered the world with them.

At a musical contest in Weiyang City, a theater master unveiled a Tang Dynasty pipa, carved entirely from stone. He Wanchun recognized it instantly: This was his family's pipa. He demanded its return, but the theater master, having paid a fortune for it, refused. As they argued, a man in his thirties appeared with a smile. "The true owner of this pipa can play it," he said. "Since both claim it, let each prove it with a song." The theater master, confident in his skill, went first. But the stone pipa was impossibly heavy. He could barely lift it. Propping it against the ground, he plucked at its strings, succeeding only in cutting his fingers. He Wanchun laughed, hoisted the pipa onto his shoulder, and strummed wildly. The notes rang for miles, though hardly melodious. Humiliated, the theater master ordered his men to seize the pipa and break He Wanchun's hands. Outnumbered, He Wanchun fought back, until the stranger intervened, revealing himself as Hu Changyi, acting master of the Masked Troupe.

Hu Changyi purchased the pipa and told He Wanchun that if he wanted it back, he must return to the Masked Troupe with him. He Wanchun had no choice but to agree. Upon arriving at the Masked Troupe, he first began studying music but ended up snapping 300 pipa strings and breaking 50 ramskin drums. He damaged every instrument in the Dewfall Barge: flutes, guqins, ruan lutes, panpipes, ramskin drums, bili pipes, yu pipes, fangxiang, pipas, and clappers. The Dewfall Barge's music master finally lost patience, deciding the boy had no musical talent and transferring him to the Snowswirl Barge where He Wanchun trained in song and dance with junior disciples, but his tone-deaf singing wrecked every melody. After several disasters, the dance master ordered him to focus only on group performances. His muscular build and gangly limbs made him anything but "light as swirling snow" in dance, and his powerful movements often meant accidental collisions with his partners. He managed modest success only in sword dances and character formation dances, while his peers avoided him like the plague. The Snowswirl Barge's dance master concluded he lacked rhythmic talent altogether. Noticing his strength, they assigned him to carry instruments and set up stages across the pavilions.

He Wanchun grew deeply frustrated, thinking he might as well return to wandering with his old opera troupe. That night, he carried the stone pipa to the lakeshore and played, pouring all his pent-up frustration into the music. Unaware of how much louder the stone pipa was than ordinary ones, his playing rippled across the water, disturbing the entire Masked Troupe's sleep and awakening Hu Changyi, who was drinking at Zephyr Pavilion. Following the sound, he found He Wanchun and learned of his struggles. Astonished, he tested He Wanchun and discovered his long, powerful fingers, keen ear, and sharp memory, ideal traits for a musician. How could the Dewfall Barge masters declare him untalented? The truth emerged when he understood He Wanchun's history with the stone pipa: Crafted by He Huaizhi, its extreme weight and rigid strings had taught the boy only brute force as a child, preventing him from mastering the subtle control needed for other instruments. His talent had been stifled by starting with the wrong tool.

Thereafter, Hu Changyi ordered He Wanchun to return to the Dewfall Barge, but with a strict condition: He must hold a chicken egg in his hand while playing. If the egg broke, it meant he was using too much force. He would only be allowed to formally study music when he could complete a piece without cracking the egg, and he was forbidden from touching the stone pipa until then. It took a full year for He Wanchun to play an entire piece with the egg intact. From there, his progress surged as he mastered every instrument and score in the Dewfall Barge. Once he could play ordinary instruments with skill, Hu returned the stone pipa to him, again requiring the chicken egg to be held. Three years later, He Wanchun finally played a piece with the stone pipa from start to finish without breaking the egg, and Hu Changyi declared him fully trained. By then, his pipa skills had made him the leading musician of the Dewfall Barge's seated orchestra division.

He Wanchun was never one to stay in one place. After notifying the troupe master, he often set out on journeys. Gradually, his fame spread throughout the land, and he became known as one of the "Six Great Performers" of the Masked Troupe.

zh:
晋王既殁，麦陵野人会合冯道，重建文津馆的希望重新燃起。他着手收集旧案，为文津馆继承前人之志，更四处寻觅证据，只为替师弟方白平反。

而这位双腿残废多年的麦陵野人，竟也在水月手中逐日好转，经脉重续，步履复常，武学大进；水月亦从其中悟得医武同源之妙。
二人相视，旧事尽付无言。正因共享了旧日颠沛与沉痛，这才形成此门武学中有如“疾风劲草”的坚韧风骨。阴霾不曾消弭，而是纳入记忆之底，迸出新生之力。
沉疴已愈，冤屈已雪。旧霾渐散，新风将至。
en:
Following the death of the Prince of Jin, the Wheat Ridge Recluse joined forces with Feng Dao, reigniting the hope of rebuilding the Inkbound Order. He began gathering old case files to ensure the Order could carry on the will of its predecessors, traveling far and wide in search of evidence to clear the name of his junior martial brother, Fang Bai.

By sheer serendipity, Moonstream, the gracious physician treating his crippled legs, turned out to be a firsthand witness to the tragedy at the Peachgrove Pass years ago. The circumstantial evidence she held finally allowed Fang Bai's unjust grievances to be cleared. Meanwhile, the Wheat Ridge Recluse, whose legs had been paralyzed for years, found his condition improving day by day under Moonstream's care. His severed meridians were reconnected, his ability to walk was restored, and his martial prowess advanced drastically. From this miraculous recovery, Moonstream also enlightened herself to the profound truth that medicine and martial arts share the exact same origin.

The two looked at each other, leaving all past sorrows to unspoken understanding. It was precisely because they had shared the turbulence and agony of the past that this martial discipline developed a resilient spirit, much like "sturdy grass standing firm in fierce winds." The gloom was never truly erased; instead, it was buried at the very bottom of their memories, bursting forth as the power of new life.

The chronic illness is cured. The unjust grievance is washed away. The old gloom gradually dissipates, and a new wind is about to arrive.

zh:
第一回·烂昭昭兮未央

话说九天之外，有一混沌幽晦之国，不得明星指引，更无日月光华，举国上下，皆陷浑噩迷蒙之中。 
忽有一日，一巡游仙人自天外云中而来，肤如凝脂，青丝如瀑，着若英采衣，携辰星披挂，执寻龙司灯，光华流转，降落凡尘，烂昭昭兮未央。 
仙人环顾四野，问曰：“此乃何地？怎不见星河高悬？”
世人惶惶，反问仙人曰：“何为星河？”
仙人叹曰：“世间竟有不知星子为何物之地？” 
言罢，仙人自披挂上摘下一星，赠与世人。倏忽间，明星灿灿，混沌开裂，幽晦之国得见天光。世人惊叹，皆伏地而拜，拥仙人为“云中君”。
仙人见此地偏僻凄寒，蒙昧可怜，心生恻隐。然有使命在身，巡游不得久留，便解下辰星披挂赐予世人，曰：“愿此星光为尔等照路。” 
仙人将披挂悬于天陉之上，顿时星斗铺天，熠熠生辉。仙人遂自云中而去，不见踪影。
然辰星之重，非常人能负。此仙人至宝，更无人可御。千百年间，辰星披挂高悬于九霄，俟有缘人撷之。

……

第十九回·聊翱游兮周章

王家小女年十九，武艺了得，身姿飒沓，下可驭轻舟行百里，上可踏清风逐明月，遨游四海，行侠仗义，荡尽不平。
某日，得闻辰星披挂高悬，已待千载。于是立誓，当登天陉、摘辰星，更以光明，周济天下。 
然天陉之路，何其险阻，需得翻过万重山岭，渡千里江泽，取浮英野之花种，浇以摇光池中天水，循天地时序悉心栽培，方能铺就通天路。
虽知其难，王氏女子仍未有犹疑，即日启程，聊翱游兮周章。 

……

第二十六回·与日月兮齐光

此去七年，风餐露宿，跋山涉水，斩落万难，终抵天陉。辰星披挂历经千百年风霜雨雪，光华渐逝，所余了了，所幸终遇有缘人愿承其重，重点天光。
所谓星子，乃天地风物所藏真理，耕织渔猎之法，机巧哲思之道，无所不有，无所不包。然虽得仙人至宝，求索真意仍为漫漫长路。自此，王氏女子身披辰星，循光指引，遍走天下，广布慧根，解民疾苦，亦得江湖名号——“云中君”。

……
en:
Part I: Brightness Without End
Beyond the Nine Heavens, so the tale goes, there lay a shadowed land, dim and unformed. No bright stars guided it, and no sun or moon cast down their light. High and low, the whole realm lay sunk in murk and confusion.
One day, a wandering immortal came down from the clouds beyond the heavens. With skin as smooth as jade and dark hair cascading like a waterfall, the immortal wore a robe adorned with flowers and stars, with constellations draped across the shoulders. The radiant glow of the Dragonfinder Lantern shimmered and shifted, bedazzling and seemingly shining without end.
The immortal looked out across the land and asked, "What place is this? Why are there no stars here?"
The people, fearful and bewildered, asked in return, "What are stars?"
The immortal sighed. "Can there truly be a place in this world that does not even know what stars are?"
With that, the immortal plucked a single star from the starry harness and gifted it to the people. In an instant, bright stars blazed forth, chaos split apart, and the darkened land beheld the light of heaven. The people marveled, fell to the ground in worship, and hailed the immortal as the Lord of Clouds.
Seeing how remote, bleak, and pitiable the place was in its ignorance, the immortal took pity on it. Yet the immortal had a duty to fulfill and could not linger long in this wandering. Thus, the immortal removed the starry cloak and bestowed it upon the people, saying, "May this starlight light your way."
The immortal hung the cloak high above the Heaven's Threshold. At once the stars spread across the sky, glittering in boundless splendor. Then, the immortal vanished back into the clouds, leaving no trace behind.
But the weight of the stars was no burden ordinary people could bear. This treasure of the immortal was beyond any mortal's power to command. And so, for hundreds upon hundreds of years, the starry cloak remained hanging high in the heavens, waiting for the one fated to claim it.

...

Part XIX: Drifting Far in Restless Flight
The Wang family's youngest daughter was only nineteen, yet already highly accomplished in martial arts, her movements swift and spirited. On water, she could steer a boat a hundred li. On land, she could ride the clear wind and chase the bright moon. She roamed the world, righting wrongs and sweeping away injustice wherever she found it.
One day, she heard that the starry cloak still hung aloft, where it had waited for a thousand years. At once, she swore that she would climb the Heaven's Threshold, seize the stars, and bring their light to all under heaven.
But the road to the Heaven's Threshold was perilous beyond measure. One had to cross ten thousand ridges, ford a thousand li of rivers and marshes, gather flower seeds from Driftseed Moor, water them with heavenly water from Alkaid Pool, and tend them with care in harmony with the seasons of Heaven and Earth. Only then could the road to the sky be laid.
Though she knew how hard it would be, the Wang daughter did not hesitate. That very day, she set out, wandering far in restless flight.
...
Part XXVI: Shining with Sun and Moon
Seven years passed in this endeavor. She endured hardship on the road, crossed mountains and rivers, and overcame countless trials until at last she reached the Heaven's Threshold. The starry cloak had weathered centuries of wind, frost, rain, and snow. Its brilliance had faded, and little remained. Yet at last, it had found one willing to bear its weight and rekindle the light of heaven.
For the stars were nothing less than the truths hidden within Heaven and Earth: the ways of farming and weaving, of fishing and hunting, the arts of craft, the principles of thought. There was nothing they did not contain, nothing they did not embrace.
Yet even with the immortal's treasure in hand, the search for its true meaning was still a long road ahead. From that day on, the Wang daughter wore the stars upon her back and followed their guiding light across the world, planting wisdom far and wide and easing the sufferings of the people. Thus, did she too gain a name in the jianghu:
Lord of Clouds.

After the flames died down, Liu Anran found a thumb ring in the rubble. She kept it as a vow, a vow to kill the coward who preyed on the helpless. 

She parted ways with her brother and became one of the Velvet Shade, a place she knew would let her take her revenge the fastest. 

There, among the Khitan, she met a woman. An older sister figure, someone burdened with shame for what her own father had done. They became friends. 

And still, Liu Anran killed the man, her friend's father. 

She left the glittering halls of Revelry Hall, returned to the dust and grit of the mortal world. Then, she opened a shop. In Kaifeng, she met that friend again, but the woman had long since shaved her head, and left all worldly ties behind.

师父总叫她遇事冷静，可她一闭上眼，那些事却总沸腾着，如这盛夏的蝉鸣。
在这隐世的山中习技是好，可她总能隐隐听见远处的哭喊。
她偏不信命，所以才能活。可每天仍有无数不信命的人接连死去。死在天灾，死在战火，死在缺饮少食，死在众生相害。
天道究竟为何？木鸢擅飞，又该如何飞往墨门期许的那个桃源？
再睁开眼时，山中依旧烈日高悬，蝉鸣不止，竟已是一天之后。
她的心中有了新的方向——在窥天之前，她要出山。
en:
Master always told her to remain calm in the face of adversity, but whenever she closed her eyes, those memories would seethe and boil, much like the chorus of midsummer cicadas.
Honing her skills in these secluded mountains was all well and good, yet she could still faintly hear the distant cries of the suffering.
She stubbornly refused to accept her fate, and that was the only reason she had survived. Yet every day, countless others who also defied their fates continued to perish one after another, falling to natural disasters, to the fires of war, to famine and drought, and to the mutual cruelty of mankind.
What exactly is the Will of Heaven? The Wooden Eagle is a master of flight, but how is it supposed to fly to the Haven envisioned by the Mohists?
When she opened her eyes again, the scorching sun still hung high over the mountains, and the cicadas chirped endlessly. An entire day had already passed.
A new direction formed in her heart: before she could divine the Will of Heaven, she first had to leave the mountain.

柒柒，曾被稚子所救，极喜爱人类。
最爱与一群稚童嬉戏玩耍，好不热闹。
他的梦想，喵生一辈子与这些孩童们相伴。
但逐渐，这群孩童都不再来了。
柒柒疑惑，四处寻觅。发现这群孩童或埋头苦读，或随父母劳作，再无往日欢笑。
柒柒上前缠着他们嬉戏玩耍，不料孩子们皆因干活读书拒绝了他。
他不理解，干活读书，难道比玩快乐吗？快乐的话为什么他们都不笑呢？
明明都是孩子，怎么不玩呢？
他想回到昔日的时光，再次看到孩子们纯真的笑颜。
en:
Sevensan was once saved by a child. Since then, he adored humans. 
He loved playing with kids—chasing, tumbling, squealing. Those were the happiest days. 
He wanted to play with them for the rest of his life. 
But slowly, the children stopped coming. 
Puzzled, Sevensan searched for them. He found them buried in books, or working beside their parents. No more giggles, no more games. 
When he tried to play with them again, they all refused him. Too much studying, too much work. 
He didn't understand—
How could studying and working be more fun than playing? If they were happy, why didn't they laugh? 
They were still kids, so why weren't they playing anymore? 
He longed to return to old times, when their smiles were so pure.

一个孩子歪着头看着，而后想着，若有两个彩色的小人，穿着绸衣，在这鼓面上踮着脚尖，一圈、又一圈地转着，该多好看。 
可这念头只打了个转儿，又落下。$T(30)想，若真有小人日日夜夜在上面打转，怕也会无聊。
左右都想不到好法子，孩子正皱眉，而远处，斗鸡的锣声“哐”一声响了。
于是那些未解的、关于花鼓和小人的畅想，也“哐”的一声，不见了。
en:
At the fair there was a beautiful drum on display. No one paid it much attention. In the end, the seller set it off to the side and turned to chat with the stall owner next door.
A child stood there looking at it for a while, then started imagining how nice it would be if two tiny painted figures in bright silk could dance across the drumhead, circling round and round on their toes.
But $T(30) soon dismissed that thought. If they really had to dance there all day, every day, would they not get bored?
The child frowned, trying to think it through, but got nowhere. Then somewhere in the distance, a gong rang out from a cockfight stall.
That was the end of that. The thought vanished as quickly as it had come.

zh:
钱，是不嫌少的。
学会这几招，让每一文钱长成一百文！

第一招：用人来赚钱
九流门少的是钱，多的是人。而人，要怎么转变成钱？答案就在梨园！
梨园弟子出演，总需要人捧场；弟子的名声，也需要人来传扬。这些人，都可以是九流门。只需召集九流门兄与阿妹，与梨园中人谈妥。试想想，一场演出一个观众十文，一百个观众就是一千文；传一句好评价五文，一百句就是五百文。
要做成这件事，最重要的是练好话术，谈高价格。届时在中间抽成，自有宝钱滚滚来。

第二招：野地里面找金子
这里的金子不是真金子，但可以变成真金子。
荒山里的野花、石缝里的杂草，它们和金子之间，只差一双能辨认的眼睛。
要问眼睛怎么练，开封城郊找医馆。
假扮学徒练出眼力，就能分辨出哪些是有用的草药，采集起来，就能卖给青溪大夫们。又学到本事又赚到钱，将来混出感情还能省下诊金，这就叫做药钱还得从大夫身上出。

第三招：一次赚两份钱
一次赚两份钱的机会虽然少，但也不是没有。
凡是雨水多的时节，就往阴暗潮湿的地方摸，多半可以摸到奇形怪状的菇。有认识的能吃的就挑出来，放集市上卖；不认识的长得乱七八糟的也挑出来，等看到面色苍白、气质阴郁的人过路时，再拿出来卖。这些人有可能是无心谷弟子，喜欢收集毒菇，必会来问价，尽管开价就是。
注意，两边不能卖混，要是出事被开封府逮去，可没人来捞。

看到这里，聪明的九流门已经小有积蓄，不必再多学。
但要真想学，老夫倒确实还有招，且去看下册！
en:
You can never have too much money. 
Learn these techniques, and turn every coin into many more! 

Technique One: Turning People into Profit 
The Nine Mortal Ways always has plenty of people but often lacks money. How can you turn people into profit? The answer lies with the Masked Troupe. 
The Masked Troupe disciples need an audience, and their reputation depends on word of mouth. Your contacts in the Nine Mortal Ways can fill these roles. Simply gather your peers and negotiate with the Masked Troupe disciples. For example, if one ticket costs ten wen and a hundred people attend, that's a thousand; a single positive review can be worth five wen, so a hundred good reviews could bring in five hundred. 
Success depends on good negotiation skills and setting fair prices. Taking a share of the proceeds will ensure a steady income. 

Technique Two: Finding Value in the Wilderness 
This kind of "gold" isn't literal gold, but it can be just as valuable. 
Wildflowers on barren hills and weeds growing between rocks all become treasures when you have the trained eye to recognize them. 
Where to train your eye? Visit a clinic on the outskirts of Kaifeng. 
Pretend to be an apprentice and learn how to identify useful medicinal herbs. Collect them and sell to Silver Needle. This way, you learn a skill and earn money—and with good relationships, you might even save on medical fees down the line. In other words, your medical expenses end up being covered by the healers you work with. 

Technique Three: Doubling Your Earnings from a Single Opportunity 
Opportunities to earn twice as much don't come often, but they do exist. 
During rainy seasons, explore damp, shadowy areas where you're likely to find oddly shaped mushrooms. Pick the edible ones to sell at the market. Hold onto unfamiliar or strange mushrooms and sell them to pale, somber passers-by—likely Hollow Vale disciples who collect poisonous mushrooms. Feel free to set your price. 
Be careful not to mix sales between regular customers and these collectors. Getting caught by the Kaifeng Prefecture could mean serious trouble, with no one coming to your aid. 

If you're smart enough, you have probably accumulated some savings by now and don't need to learn more. 
But if you're eager to keep learning, I do have additional secrets. Look for the next volume!
